passage: Late evening in the hostel common room, Avni noticed Kashish's chair empty for the third night. Kashish's post about a college cricket match had been picked up by strangers who mocked her all day, and her door stayed shut. Avni did not knock with advice. She sent a private message: "No need to answer. I'm here. What would help right now? I can read the comments so you don't have to." An hour later a reply came: "Could you just sit with me?" Avni brought two cups of tea and sat on the floor by the bed, saying almost nothing. She resisted the urge to post a defence under the thread. Near midnight Kashish said, "Thanks for not fixing it."

qa.q: What did Avni offer to do with the comments?
qa.a: She offered to read the comments so Kashish wouldn't have to.

qa.q: Why did Avni hold back from posting a defence under the thread?
qa.a: Avni felt protective of Kashish but held back, sensing that quiet presence would help more than adding public noise to the mocking thread.

qa.q: What else could Avni do over the next few days to support Kashish?
qa.a: Keep asking what would help, offer again to check the messages, and stay nearby without pushing advice.

qa.q: What might Kashish have meant by "Thanks for not fixing it"?
qa.a: Kashish was probably relieved to be listened to without advice. Company felt more helpful than solutions while sinking under the mockery.

grounding: A friend is being trolled and sinking; a private message, asking what help is wanted, offering to read messages and just being present.

passage:
"When Shreya's video went viral, I'm Ishita, her roommate from college, and I just remember how she went quiet. Not crying. Quiet.

The comments were horrible. Hundreds of strangers about her face, her accent. Our friends were all posting public defences, arguing with trolls under her post. Which made it bigger.

I didn't know what to do, so I messaged her privately. Just: 'I'm here. What would help right now? You don't have to answer.'

She wrote back two hours later: 'Can you read my messages for me? I can't look.'

So I did. Every night for a week I went through her inbox, deleted the vile ones, saved the threatening ones for reporting, and sent her only the kind notes.

I didn't give her a list of advice. I just stayed. She told me later that was the thing that kept her standing."

qa.q: What did Shreya ask Ishita to do?
qa.a: To read her messages for her, because she couldn't look.

qa.q: What does Shreya's quietness suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt overwhelmed and hurt, sinking under hundreds of strangers' cruel comments.

qa.q: Why did Ishita's private message help more than public defences?
qa.a: It asked what Shreya wanted without piling advice, and it led to practical help like checking her messages, instead of making the attack bigger.

qa.q: How does Shreya see Ishita's help?
qa.a: Shreya saw Ishita's steady presence as the thing that kept her standing during the trolling.

grounding: The spoken account shows a friend who, when someone close is trolled, messages privately, asks what help they want, checks the messages for them and stays present instead of defending them publicly.

passage:
Monday. Thomas saw Manjula's post about her small tailoring business had been picked up by a hate page. Hundreds of comments mocked her as a "loser who can't sew." He wanted to jump in and argue with every one. Instead he sent her a private text: "Saw it. I'm so sorry. Do you want me to do anything, or just be around?"

Wednesday. Manjula hadn't posted in two days. She called him, voice thin. "I keep reading them. I can't stop." Thomas asked, "Want me to go through them for you? I'll save anything threatening and you don't have to see the rest."

"Yes. Please."

Saturday. He'd sorted it all. Two threats were reported. The rest he just deleted. He took her for dosa and didn't bring up the comments once.

She laughed for the first time that week. "You didn't lecture me," she said. "I noticed."

qa.q: What did the hate page call Manjula?
What was Thomas feeling when he first saw the comments?
qa.a: He felt angry and protective, wanting to argue with every commenter.

qa.q: What did Thomas do that helped Manjula most?
qa.a: He asked privately what she wanted, offered to check the messages for her, reported the threats and simply spent time with her without lecturing.

qa.q: How does Manjula see Thomas's support?
qa.a: Manjula feels relieved and cared for, noticing and appreciating that he didn't lecture her 🤍.

grounding: Across several days, the passage shows a friend who reaches out privately to someone being trolled, asks what help they want, checks messages for them and stays present without piling advice.
